questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Why did Mahatma Gandhiji travel to Champaran in Bihar in 1917?
questions.answer: In 1916 Gandhiji travelled to Champaran in Bihar to inspire the peasants to struggle against the oppressive plantation system. Then in 1917, he organised a Satyagraha to support the peasants of the Kheda district of Gujarat.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Explain the importance of National Highways in India.
questions.answer: National Highways link extreme parts of the country. These are the primary road systems which facilitate the transportation of people and goods.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How is one-party system different from two-party system? Explain with examples.
questions.answer: One-Party System: Only one political party runs the government. Example: China. Two-Party System: Two parties compete in elections. Example: USA.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How do double coincidence of wants arise?
questions.answer: When there is no medium of exchange, the buyer must find a seller who wants the same good the buyer offers. This is double coincidence of wants.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Why did Mahatma Gandhi decide to withdraw the Non-cooperation Movement in February 1922? Explain. (Or)
questions.answer: In Feb 1922, Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation movement because: (i) The movement was turning violent in many places. (ii) Satyagrahis needed proper training before struggles.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How did the First World War create a new economic situation in India? Explain.
questions.answer: WWI created: (i) Increased defence expenditure financed by war loans and raised taxes; prices almost doubled. (ii) Forced recruitment caused widespread anger. (iii) Crop failures created food shortages.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Analyse the outcomes of democracies in terms of economic growth and development.
questions.answer: Outcomes: (a) Democracy eradicates unhelpful programmes. (b) Reduces economic disparities. (c) Encourages freedom and dignity, creating peace for economic prosperity.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Explain the three important terms of Credit.
questions.answer: Terms: (i) Interest Rate - decided while borrowing/lending. (ii) Collateral - asset owned by borrower as guarantee. (iii) Documentation - employment and income records checked.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Examine any five major challenges faced by the political parties in India. (Or)
questions.answer: Challenges: (i) Lack of internal democracy. (ii) No regular membership registers, meetings, or internal elections. (iii) Dynastic succession. (iv) Growing money and muscle power. (v) No meaningful choice to voters.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: "Political parties play an important role in democratic countries." Justify the statement.
questions.answer: Parties are necessary: (i) Democracies cannot exist without parties. (ii) No candidate can make policy promises independently. (iii) Government utility uncertain without parties. (iv) No one responsible for running the country. (v) Agencies needed to gather and present views.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How are our markets transformed in recent years? Explain with examples. (Or)
questions.answer: Markets transformed: (i) Global production and international sales. (ii) Interlinked locations. (iii) Integration of markets through foreign trade. (iv) More movement of goods, services, investments, technology. (v) Faster delivery at lower costs through technology.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How do Multi National Corporations (MNCs) interlink production across countries? Explain with examples.
questions.answer: MNCs: (i) Set up in regions with cheap labour (China, India). (ii) Joint production with local companies. (iii) Buy up local companies (Cargill bought Parakh Foods). (iv) Place orders with small producers, sell under own brand.

questions.subject: Social Science

questions.answer: Gandhiji organised a non-violent movement in South Africa. He established South African Indian Congress.

questions.subject: Social Science

questions.answer: Satyagraha is pure soul-force because it emphasises truth and is against violence.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Read the case on Satyagraha - (iii) How has Gandhiji described passive resistance?
questions.answer: Passive resistance means soul force or truth force. It is a method of securing rights by personal suffering with no ill-will.

questions.subject: Social Science

questions.subject: Social Science

questions.answer: Agro-industries boost agriculture productivity; industries depend on agriculture for raw materials (cotton textile); industries provide inputs (fertilisers, machines); transport helps farmers.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
questions.question: "Ideas of national unity in early 19th century Europe were allied to liberalism." Examine.
questions.answer: Liberalism = freedom, equality before law, end of aristocracy; constitutional government; voting only for property-owning men; economic freedom - free markets, customs union by Prussia (1834), railways stimulated unification.

questions.subject: Social Science

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How is IT connected with globalization?
questions.answer: IT connects countries; jobs outsourced; production spread across countries; internet for orders, design, payment; e-commerce, e-banking, e-learning, e-governance.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Analyze the need of Political Parties in democracy.
questions.answer: Without parties, no major policy changes, no responsible government. Parties gather views, present to government, bring representatives together, support/restrain government. Essential for democracy.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Why is Tertiary Sector becoming important in India? (Or)

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Examine the progress of Civil Disobedience Movement in countryside. (Or)

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Analyze how people of different communities developed a sense of collective belonging in India.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How is pipeline transport network important in India? Explain with example. (Or)

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How have physical and economic factors influenced Indian Railway Network distribution?
questions.answer: Physiographic: Plains have dense network; mountains, deserts, swamps have sparse. Economic: Rich resource regions have denser network. Administrative: Political decisions affect distribution.

questions.subject: Social Science

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: "Workers of Assam had their own understanding of Swaraj." Explain. (Or ZZYY1/6)

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How can industrial pollution of fresh water be reduced? (Or ZZYY1/6)
questions.answer: (i) Minimise water use by reusing/recycling. (ii) Rainwater harvesting. (iii) Treat effluents: Primary (mechanical), Secondary (biological), Tertiary (biological/chemical/physical with recycling).

questions.subject: Social Science

questions.subject: Social Science

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How is Democracy better than dictatorship? (Or ZZYY1/6)

questions.subject: Social Science

questions.answer: Protect endangered species by banning hunting, giving legal protection to habitats, restricting wildlife trade.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: (iii) How are communities working for wildlife conservation? Example?

questions.subject: Social Science

questions.subject: Social Science

questions.answer: By increasing Women representation and voice in democracy.

questions.subject: Social Science

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: "The assertion of social diversities in a democratic country is very normal and can be healthy." Justify the statement with argument.
questions.answer: Assertion of social diversities in a country need not be seen as a source of danger because in a democratic country every person and a community has the right to state their views and opinions. This is very normal and healthy in a democracy. This allows the less privileged and marginal groups to express their grievances and concerns and can get the government to attend to these. This only leads to the strengthening of democracy.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: 'Social division affects politics' OR When does a social difference become a social division?
questions.answer: In general, we belong to a community because we were born into it. This leads to us being born with social differences that already exist. Social differences are also based on the choices we make due to our cultural and professional life. Social difference which may cause one community to be at a disadvantage as compared to another community, leading to a feeling of discrimination. This produces tension among the communities and are pitted against one another. This produces social divisions.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: What was the aim of the Civil Rights Movement in the USA?
questions.answer: The Civil Rights movement aimed at abolition of legal racial discrimination against African-Americans.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Who were Afro-Americans?
questions.answer: Afro-American, Black-American or Black are the terms used to refer mainly to the descendants of Africans who were brought into America as slaves between the 17th century and early 19th century.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Differentiate between overlapping difference and cross-cutting difference. Give example from Netherlands and Northern Ireland.
questions.answer: Overlapping differences lead to social division because some social differences overlap with other differences. They are difficult to accommodate. In Northern Ireland, Christians are divided between Catholics and Protestants. Here class and religion overlap with each other. Catholics are poor and have faced discrimination. This has resulted in conflicts. Cross-cutting differences do not lead to social divisions because it is difficult to pit one group of people against the other. They are easier to accommodate as in the case of Netherlands. In the Netherlands, class and religion tend to cut across each other. Catholics and Protestants are equally likely to be poor or rich. So they do not have conflicts so their differences are easily accommodated.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: "Every social difference does not lead to social division." Explain.
questions.answer: (i) It is true that every social difference does not lead to social division. Social differences divide similar people from one another, but they also unite very different people. (ii) People belonging to different social groups share differences and similarities cutting across the boundaries of their groups. (iii) It is also fairly common for people belonging to same religion to feel that they do not belong to the same community due to different castes or sects. Similarly it is possible for people from different religions to have the same caste and feel close to each other. (iv) Rich and poor persons from the same family do not have close relations with each other. They feel that they are different.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Social divisions of one kind or the other exist in most countries. Explain with examples.
questions.answer: (i) Social divisions of one kind or the other exist in most countries: (a) In India there are many communities - Hindu, Muslims, Sikh, Christians etc. (b) Belgium is a small country with many communities - French, Dutch and German speaking. (c) Germany and Sweden with no significant ethnic differences have influx of people from other parts of the world. Migrants bring their own culture and form a different social community. (ii) There are people of different castes in countries like India. Caste too leads to social divisions. (iii) Society is divided on the basis of status i.e. rich, poor, literate and illiterate. For example, we find a wide gap between the rich and the poor in India, particularly in rural areas. (iv) There may be social divisions on the basis of culture too as in India.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Give negative effects in which social divisions affect politics.
questions.answer: (i) In Northern Ireland 53 per cent Protestants and 44 per cent Catholics were represented by the Unionists and Nationalists respectively. (ii) Nationalists demanded that Northern Ireland be unified with the Republic of Ireland - a Catholic country. (iii) The Unionists wanted to remain with the UK, a Protestant country. (iv) This resulted in a conflict between Unionists and Nationalists. (v) It was only in 1998 that the UK government and the Nationalists reached an agreement leading to suspension of struggle. (vi) In Yugoslavia, the political competition along the religious and ethnic lines led to the disintegration of Yugoslavia into six independent states.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: In a democracy, "every expression of social divisions in politics is not disastrous." Establish the truth of the statement with the help of an example. OR "In a democracy, political expression of social divisions is normal and can be healthy." Support this statement by giving three suitable arguments.
questions.answer: (i) Social divisions exist in most countries of the world. These divisions are reflected in politics. (ii) The assertion of social diversities in a country need not be seen as a source of danger because in a democracy, political expression of social divisions is very normal and can be healthy. This allows disadvantaged and marginal social groups to express their grievances and get the government to attend to these. (iii) In a democracy political parties discuss these divisions and make different promises to communities and make policies to redress the grievances of the disadvantaged communities. (iv) Expression of various kinds of social divisions in politics often results in their cancelling one another out and thus reducing their intensity. This leads to strengthening of a democracy.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How are issue-specific movements different from generic movements?
questions.answer: Issue-specific movements seek to achieve a single objective within a limited time. For example, Narmada Bachao Andolan in India. Generic movements seek to achieve a broad goal in very long time. For example, women's movements.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How do pressure groups and movements exert influence on politics? Explain with examples.
questions.answer: The activities of pressure groups and movements exert influence on politics as well as democracy in a variety of ways: (i) By gaining public support and sympathy through information campaigns, organising meetings, filing petitions. (ii) By playing the role of invisible and unofficial government - they protect collective interests and try to influence those in power like ministers, bureaucrats and politicians. (iii) By forming linkage between masses and the elite - they articulate the claims of their members and become a means of communication between the masses and the elite. (iv) By organising protest activities in the form of strikes, hartals, bandhs. (v) By forming political parties and providing leadership - for example, the formation of Asom Gana Parishad out of the Assam Movement.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: 'The democracy has been evolved through struggles and movements all over the world.' Support the statement with examples.
questions.answer: Popular movements deepen democracy by ensuring greater participation of people through meetings and processions, making people more aware and vigilant. They help in the due representation and accommodation of diverse interests. They put pressure on the government making it more accountable and responsive. The examples of Nepal and Bolivia show the power of the common people involving mass mobilisation, public demonstrations, agitation. It shows that people from different walks of life can form an organisation and base their struggle for fairness.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: 'The popular struggles are integral to the development of democracy.' Analyse the statement.
questions.answer: Struggles are essential to save democracy, for example, Nepal's struggle for restoration of democracy and Bolivia's water war against privatisation. It is only through struggles that diverse groups can express their feelings. If people disagree with government policies, they can oppose through struggle to achieve their goals. Struggles keep democracy in working mode and keep the government in check.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How are popular struggles integral to the working of democracy? Explain with an example of Bolivia's struggle against privatisation of water.
questions.answer: Popular struggles do not end with the establishment of democracy, they are an integral part of a democracy because democracy evolves through popular struggles. In Bolivia, the democratically-elected government undermined the welfare of the people by handing over the water supply right to an MNC. People resorted to protest. It is only in democracy that people can express their opinions. If people do not agree with government policies, they have the right to oppose them.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: What inspiration do we get from Bolivia's popular struggle? Explain any three values.
questions.answer: (i) Determination - even after being brutally treated by the police, the people in Bolivia did not stop their struggle. (ii) Cooperation and support - the protest involved local professionals, engineers, environmentalists, factory workers' union, students and homeless children working together. (iii) Perseverance and steadfastness - people had the courage to defy their own government and the MNC.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Compare the popular struggles of Nepal and Bolivia.
questions.answer: Dissimilarities: (i) The movement in Nepal was to establish democracy, while the struggle in Bolivia involved claims on an elected, democratic government. (ii) Nepal movement was about fundamental change in form of government - transition from monarchy to democracy. Bolivia's struggle was about one specific issue - against privatisation of water supply. (iii) In Nepal, the struggle was led by SPA supported by Maoists. In Bolivia, it was led by FEDECOR which was not a political party. Similarities: Both had political conflict leading to popular struggles and mass mobilisation. Both were successful.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Describe the popular struggle of Bolivia.
questions.answer: Bolivia is a poor country in South America. The World Bank pressurised the government to give up its control of municipal water supply. The government sold these rights for Cochabamba to an MNC which immediately increased water price four times. This resulted in spontaneous protest. In January 2000, a new alliance organised a successful four-day general strike. The government promised negotiation but nothing happened. Another strike in February - police brutality. In April, strike again and martial law. The power of people forced MNC officials to flee the city. The contract was cancelled and water supply restored at old rates. This was Bolivia's water war.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Describe the movement for democracy in Nepal, April 2006.
questions.answer: The movement aimed at restoring democracy. King Birendra, who accepted constitutional monarchy, was killed in the royal massacre of 2001. King Gyanendra was not prepared to accept democratic rule. He dismissed the Prime Minister and dissolved parliament. All major parties formed SPA and called for a four-day strike in Kathmandu. Maoists and others joined and the strike turned indefinite with around 5 lakh protestors. The king was forced to concede: restoration of parliament, power to an all-party government, formation of a new constituent assembly. Girija Prasad Koirala was chosen new Prime Minister. Most powers of the king were taken away.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which logo of quality is marked on the gold jewellery?
questions.answer: Hallmark is the official quality mark stamped on articles made of gold.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Give an example of violation of consumer's right to choose.
questions.answer: A common example is when a cooking gas supplier forces a new customer to buy a stove from them as a condition for providing a connection. This denies the customer the freedom to choose.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How is the maximum retail price printed on packets beneficial for you?
questions.answer: The Maximum Retail Price (MRP) printed on packets prevents sellers from charging more than the stated price. This protects consumers from being overcharged and ensures price transparency.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Give any one example of consumer's 'right to choose.'
questions.answer: If a customer wants to buy a particular brand of toothpaste but the shopkeeper insists they must also buy a toothbrush, the shopkeeper is violating the customer's right to choose.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: If you want to extract information about the functions of any government department, which right would you exercise?
questions.answer: Right to Information (R.T.I.)

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: In what condition is the 'Right to Seek Redressal' exercised? Give an example.
questions.answer: The Right to Seek Redressal is exercised when a consumer suffers loss or damage due to defective goods, deficient services or unfair trade practices. Example: Mahesh sent a money order to his daughter for her marriage but the money never reached her on time. He filed a case in the district consumer court.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: If any damage is done to a consumer by a trader, under which consumer right one can move to consumer court to get compensation?
questions.answer: Right to seek redressal.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Suppose you have to buy a packed bottle for drinking water in your journey. Which logo will you like to see to be sure about its quality?
questions.answer: ISI logo.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: What is the duty of a consumer?
questions.answer: Consumers should check product details such as quality, price and warranty before buying. They should also keep purchase receipts and guarantee cards as proof for any future complaint.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Name the levels of consumer courts that are available to appeal.
questions.answer: Consumer courts exist at three levels: district, state and national.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which logo will you like to see on the electric heater to be sure of its quality?
questions.answer: ISI logo.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: What is COPRA? When was it introduced?
questions.answer: COPRA stands for the Consumer Protection Act. It was enacted in 1986 to protect the interests of consumers.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which logo would you like to see for purchasing electrical goods?
questions.answer: ISI mark.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Suppose your parents want to purchase gold jewellery along with you, then which logo will you look for on the jewellery?
questions.answer: Hallmark.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How can consumers use their 'Right to Seek Redressal'? Explain with example.
questions.answer: Consumers have the right to seek redressal against unfair trade practices and exploitation. Complaints are filed depending on claim amount: District Forum up to Rs 20 lakh, State Commission Rs 20 lakh to Rs 1 crore, National Commission above Rs 1 crore. Example: Ravi bought an SUV from a dealer with warranty. The vehicle didn't have advertised features. Dealer ignored requests, so Ravi filed in district consumer court which found in his favour and awarded full compensation.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Highlight any three rights of consumers.
questions.answer: (i) Right to be informed - consumers have the right to know full particulars about goods and services before purchase including quality, quantity, price, ingredients and any risks. (ii) Right to choose - consumers have freedom to select goods and services according to their needs. They should not be forced to buy unwanted items. (iii) Right to seek redressal - consumers have the right to approach consumer forums for redressal against unfair trade practices.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How can consumer awareness be spread among consumers to avoid exploitation in the marketplace? Explain any three ways.
questions.answer: (i) Public information campaigns - government and consumer organisations use posters, pamphlets and TV ads to explain consumer rights. (ii) Education and local workshops - schools, colleges and community centres run sessions to teach about quality marks, reading labels, keeping receipts. (iii) Use of media and online platforms - newspapers, radio, social media share information on how to file complaints and how consumer courts work.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Explain with an example the impact of the Right to Information (R.T.I.).
questions.answer: In October 2005, India enacted the Right to Information Act which gives citizens access to information about the functioning of government departments. RTI enables citizens to monitor the progress of government schemes and holds officials accountable. It has helped curb corruption and can reveal flaws in selection processes or misuse of funds.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Explain with an example how one can exercise the 'Right to Choose.'
questions.answer: The consumer has the right to choose goods and services that offer fair quality, proper service and reasonable price. For example, if a shop owner insists that you must buy a toothbrush when you only want toothpaste, your right to choose is being denied. In such situations, consumers can seek redressal through the Consumer Court under COPRA.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How do large companies manipulate the markets? Explain.
questions.answer: Large companies can manipulate markets in various ways: (i) They may use their financial strength to control supply and influence prices. (ii) They can promote misleading advertisements or influence media to create unfair advantages. (iii) They may pressure smaller competitors or influence regulations to suit their interests. (iv) Historical examples include companies making false health claims about products until regulation forced corrections.
